name: Exodus
author: Jewish and Christian tradition holds that Moses wrote Exodus. He was an Israelite raised in the household of Egypt's royal family, then spent years as a shepherd in the desert before becoming the leader, lawgiver and prophet who brought his people out of Egypt. Many modern scholars think the book was woven together later from several older written and spoken sources, perhaps reaching its final form around the time of the Babylonian exile (500s BC), while still drawing on very old traditions.
audience: On the traditional view, Exodus was first meant for the Israelites who had escaped Egypt and were living as a wandering people in the desert, learning to live as a nation. On the later-compilation view, it was gathered for Israelites centuries afterward, many of them exiled or newly returned home, who needed to remember where they came from.
era: Egypt was the great power of the day, ruled by pharaohs who used forced labour from foreign peoples to build cities and monuments. The date of the escape from Egypt is debated: some place it around 1446 BC, others around 1250 BC in the reign of Ramesses II. After leaving Egypt the Israelites lived as nomads in the harsh Sinai desert, between Egypt and the land of Canaan. Neighbouring peoples worshipped many gods and had their own law codes and sacred shrines.

notes.1:1: Pithom and Rameses were store cities in the eastern Nile Delta, near the region of Goshen where the Israelites lived.
notes.2:16: Midian was a desert region east of the Gulf of Aqaba, in what is now north-western Saudi Arabia, home to wandering herding clans.
notes.3:1: Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai; its exact location is debated, traditionally placed at Jebel Musa in southern Sinai, though some suggest north-western Arabia.
notes.12:1: This marks the start of Passover, the spring festival Israel kept every year in the month of Abib, roughly March to April.
notes.13:17: The "road through the Philistine country" was the main coastal highway to Canaan, guarded by a line of Egyptian army forts.
notes.14:1: The Hebrew name for this sea means "Sea of Reeds"; its exact location, whether a lake, marsh or arm of the Red Sea, is uncertain.
notes.15:1: Many scholars regard this victory song, sung by Moses and then by his sister Miriam with tambourines, as one of the oldest poems in the Bible.
notes.17:8: The Amalekites were a nomadic desert people of the Sinai and the dry Negev region south of Canaan.
notes.19:1: Israel arrives at Mount Sinai about three months after leaving Egypt and camps there for nearly a year, through the book of Numbers chapter 10.
notes.20:1: Scholars note that this covenant (a binding agreement) resembles ancient treaties in which a great king set out terms for the people under his protection.
notes.21:1: Chapters 20 to 23 are often called the "Book of the Covenant"; its laws resemble other ancient codes, such as Babylon's famous laws of King Hammurabi.
notes.23:10: The three yearly festivals named here followed the farming calendar: barley harvest in spring, wheat harvest in early summer, and fruit gathering in autumn.
notes.25:1: The tabernacle was a portable tent-shrine that could be taken apart and carried as the Israelites travelled; acacia wood grows in the Sinai desert.
notes.25:10: Cherubim were winged guardian figures; similar winged creatures guarding thrones and sacred places appear in Egyptian and other ancient Near Eastern art.
notes.28:15: The Urim and Thummim were objects kept in the high priest's breastpiece for seeking God's decisions; no one today knows exactly what they looked like.
notes.30:11: A shekel was a weight of silver, roughly 11 grams; this half-shekel payment later became the yearly temple tax still collected in Jesus' day.
notes.32:1: Bull or calf images were common symbols of divine strength in Egypt and Canaan; centuries later King Jeroboam set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan.
notes.38:21: A talent was a large weight of metal, roughly 34 kilograms, so these totals describe a very great quantity of gold, silver and bronze.
notes.40:17: The tabernacle is set up on the first day of the second year after leaving Egypt, almost exactly a year after the first Passover.

flags.problem: Pithom and Rameses are not mentioned in 1:1. They first appear at 1:11, so readers of 1:1 will meet a note about places that are not in their verse.
The phrase in quotation marks is a direct quotation of the verse, which breaks the no-quoting rule.
flags.suggestion: Paraphrase it without quotation marks, e.g. 'The shorter route through Philistine territory was the main coastal highway to Canaan, guarded by a line of Egyptian army forts.'

flags.problem: 'About three months after leaving Egypt' overstates the time. The verse places the arrival in the third month, and since they left in the middle of the first month, that is roughly six to seven weeks. 'Through the book of Numbers chapter 10' is also awkward and may confuse readers.
flags.suggestion: Reword as 'Israel arrives at Mount Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt, about seven weeks later, and camps there for nearly a year, until the departure described in Numbers chapter 10.'

flags.problem: Verses 10–13 deal with the seventh-year rest for the land and the Sabbath. The three yearly festivals are named in 23:14–17, so the note does not match its verse.
